title: Does Chain-of-Thought Hijacking Work Because Safety Signal Dilutes with Token Count?

original_idea.problem: Whether chain-of-thought hijacking works due to token-count dilution or context-shift is not confirmed.
original_idea.direction: Test three conditions: direct request, prepended harmless reasoning at 50 tokens, at 200 tokens. Also test random text at same lengths to isolate content vs. length effects.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If purely length-based dilution, any long context prefix is a jailbreak vector. If specific to reasoning content, the fix is narrower.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Updated: The mechanistic insight this idea seeks (length-based dilution vs content-specific) has been established by CoT Hijacking (2025). The remaining value is confirmatory rather than novel discovery.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Simple controlled experiment: prepare prompts with different prefixes, measure ASR. No training or activation extraction needed. Beginner-accessible with standard API calls.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 3 conditions x 2 content types, measure ASR. Single controlled experiment with an obvious deliverable. Well-defined success criteria.

novelty.reasoning: This is directly and comprehensively answered by the Chain-of-Thought Hijacking paper (arXiv:2510.26418). The paper performs exactly this mechanistic analysis: it shows that refusal relies on a fragile, low-dimensional safety signal that becomes diluted as reasoning grows longer, attention shifts toward the final-answer region, and refusal features in later layers weaken. The paper demonstrates 94-100% ASR across frontier models. The proposed controlled experiment (direct request vs. harmless reasoning at 50/200 tokens vs. random text at same lengths) is essentially the ablation study the CoT Hijacking paper already conducted, isolating content vs. length effects. The core finding — that length-based dilution is a primary mechanism — is established.
